title: Volume of Prisms
subtitle: Length times width times height, and why that works.
objectives: Calculate the volume of a cube and a rectangular prism
Explain why the formula is a multiplication of three lengths
Find a missing edge when the volume is known

cards.title: Three numbers multiplied. That is the whole thing
cards.text: Volume of a box is length × width × height. The interesting question is why, and the answer makes the formula impossible to forget.

cards.title: Count a layer, then count the layers
cards.text: Fill the base with unit cubes, then stack that layer.
points: **The base** holds length × width cubes.
**Each layer is identical.**
**There are 'height' layers.**
**So the total is length × width × height.**

question.text: A box is 5 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. Volume in cm³? Digits only.
question.explain: 5 × 3 = 15 cubes in the base layer, and two layers: 30 cm³.

cards.title: Press an edge. Watch a cube grow
cards.text: A cube is the special case where all three edges match, so the volume is the edge cubed.

cards.title: The special case
cards.text: When all three edges are equal, the formula collapses.
points: **Edge × edge × edge** is edge³.
**A 4 cm cube** is 4³ = 64 cm³.
**That is why** the power of 3 is called cubing.
**Same formula**, fewer numbers to carry.

cards.title: Flood defences are sized by volume
cards.text: A retention pond has to hold a storm. Engineers work out how many cubic metres before anything is dug.
points: **Expected rainfall × catchment area** gives the volume.
**The pond is then sized** to take it.
**Undersize it by a third** and it overtops.
**Length × width × depth**, at civil-engineering scale.

question.text: A cube has 3 cm edges. Its volume is…
question.explain: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cm³. Nine would be the area of one face.

cards.title: Measuring the box a fan came in
cards.text: Packaging volume is the first place most people meet this formula for real.
points: **Measure three edges** in the same unit.
**Multiply all three.**
**A 60 × 40 × 25 cm box** is 60,000 cm³ — about 60 litres.
**Shipping is priced on volume**, not just weight.

cards.title: Volume known, one edge missing
cards.text: Divide instead of multiply. The formula runs both ways.
points: **Volume ÷ (the two known edges)** gives the third.
**60 cm³, base 5 × 3** → 60 ÷ 15 = 4 cm tall.
**Check by multiplying back.**
**Same relationship**, rearranged.

question.text: A prism has volume 48 cm³ and a base of 4 cm by 3 cm. How tall is it, in cm? Digits only.

cards.title: Inventory space is volume maths
cards.text: Games that use grid inventories are making you solve packing problems.
points: **A 2 × 1 item** takes two squares. In 3D it takes volume.
**Bigger containers** multiply in all directions.
**Tetris is the two-dimensional version** of the same question.
**Fitting things in a box** is a real and old problem.

terms.def: A box shape with six rectangular faces.
A rectangular prism whose edges are all equal.
A unit of volume, written with a small 3.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Volume = length × width × height.
It works because you are counting one layer, then the layers.
A cube is the case where all three edges match: edge³.
Known volume, missing edge? Divide.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 9 Math, the first of two weeks on the volume of prisms. The formula is derived rather than issued: fill the base with unit cubes, then count the layers, which is why three lengths get multiplied. That derivation is what makes it stick and also explains the cubic unit, so both are taught in one move. The cube is presented as the special case rather than a separate formula, which connects straight back to the exponent weeks. Working backwards gets its own card since a missing-edge question is standard in exams and panics anyone who memorised only one direction.
discussion: Why do you multiply three lengths rather than add them?
Why is a cube's volume written as a power?
How would you find a missing height?
extension: Measure a cereal box and work out its volume in cm³ and in litres.
Find a cube-shaped object and check the edge-cubed rule.
misconceptions: Adding the three edges instead of multiplying.
Thinking the missing-edge case needs a new formula.
